title: Collapsing Pakistan
byline: compiled and edited by Dr. N.S. Rajaram · Voice of India · c. 2001
lede: A short collection on a single prediction. N.S. Rajaram argues that Pakistan is a small productive Punjab trying to rule a vast, lawless frontier with Islam as its only glue, and that the state was heading for collapse. He builds on two pieces of reporting from 2000, which the book reprints: Robert Kaplan's tour of Quetta, Peshawar and Karachi for The Atlantic, and Jeffrey Goldberg's weeks inside the Haqqania madrasa, a school that trained many Taliban leaders.
facts: pieces: Rajaram's essay and two magazine reports from 2000
Pakistan's population in 2000, growing 2.6% a year, per Kaplan
students at the Haqqania madrasa, which placed more graduates in the Taliban leadership than any other school
Pakistan's nuclear tests, celebrated with roadside monuments
note: Rajaram's essay is a forecast written from an Indian nationalist standpoint. The two reports are American journalism, summarised briefly here. Events after the book are added and marked “since the book”, so the forecast can be checked against what happened.

sections.title: A Punjabi core and an unruly frontier
sections.lede: Rajaram takes his framework from Kaplan: Pakistan is not one nation but a core holding down its edges, held together only by Islam and by enmity with India.

items: Run by a Punjabi elite with Mohajir allies, such as Musharraf
Defines itself only against India, which a Pakistani journalist tells Kaplan is “our tragedy”
Run on smuggling, heroin and tribal law
Open to the Taliban networks Pakistan itself created

sections.after: His prediction: Pakistan would not fall quietly like the Soviet Union but break up violently like Yugoslavia, shrinking to Punjab east of the Indus, which in his view should “rejoin India its natural home”.

sections.title: Three cities, three fault lines
items: Drought, a Pashtun separatist party raided by the army, and strikes against taxing cross-border smuggling. A tribal chief says the state wants to end the tribal system “but there are no institutions to replace it”.
Doubled to a million people in the 1980s with Afghan refugees and the heroin route. Sectarian violence follows the tribal divides.
14 million people, only a quarter of them native Sindhis, and at least a quarter living in katchi abadis (makeshift houses). Contract killers committed 629 murders in ten months of 1998, none solved.

sections.title: “One group imprisons another, only to be imprisoned itself”
sections.lede: Kaplan's summary of Pakistani politics, with the Afghan story running alongside it.
items: A boundary the Pashtuns never accepted.
The frontier's few entrepreneurs, mostly Hindus, leave.
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto comes to power.
Major Farouk Adam Khan spends five years in prison, part of it in Attock Fort. By 2000 he is Musharraf's prosecutor.
After a rigged election and martial law. Zia allies the army with Sunni radicals.
The CIA finances it and the ISI manages it. Foreign money hides Pakistan's weakness, Rajaram says.
Zia dies in an air crash
Benazir Bhutto is elected. Her husband's thefts undermine her government.
Runs the country “as a family enterprise”, according to Kaplan.
Hamid Karzai tells Kaplan he helped them, until Pakistani intelligence took over the movement.
They go on to hold 80% of Afghanistan.
Sharif is later arraigned at Attock Fort.
Pakistan becomes a US ally against the Taliban, and money flows again.
Pakistan has not broken up as the book predicted, though Baluchistan and the frontier remain insurgent.

sections.title: A day at the Haqqania madrasa
sections.lede: Goldberg enrolled for some weeks at the school of Maulana Samiul Haq, a Deobandi politician who gave Mullah Omar the school's only honorary degree.
items: Funded by wealthy Pakistanis and Gulf donors. The students are mostly very poor.
In Arabic, a language the youngest boys do not understand.
Students cheer the idea of Osama bin Laden with a nuclear bomb.
Many graduates join the Taliban, and Kashmir is presented as jihad.
